The Bird Mound, erroneously named because of its vaguely bird-like shape and known to archaeologists more formally as Mound A, is the largest single structure at Poverty Point in northeast Louisiana. Standing at the cosmological center of the site, it was the monumental hub of the earliest largest scale sedentary society in North America, with a history predating the Olmec of Mesoamerica by two centuries. The Bird Mound itself was built sometime after 1450 BC, and despite its massive size, took only a few months to complete. At 238,000 cubic meters, it was the largest earthen pyramid in North America until Monks Mound was constructed nearly 2500 years later. After a thousand years of dominating the lower Mississippi culturally, economically, and ceremonially, Poverty Point went into decline around 700 BC, but its legacy of monumental construction would live in among later mound-building societies.

When the Hopewell Interaction Sphere collapsed around AD 400, most societies throughout the Eastern Woodlands ceased constructing elaborate earthworks as previous generations did. The Troyville Culture in the lower Mississippi is a notable exception. They not only continued to build earthworks, but at the eponymous Troyville site, they constructed what would be the tallest man-made structure in the region for centuries. At 25 meters tall, the Great Mound of Troyville towered over all other earthen pyramids in its day and would not be surpassed until the construction of Monks Mound. It consisted of two flat tiers topped with a steep conical mound. Its internal structure was also unique, employing reed mats to prevent slumping. Unfortunately, the Great Mound. Throughout the 1800s, the Great Mound was continually demolished to build rifle pits during the Civil War and to level the terrain as the town of Jonesville grew up around the site. Today, the Great Mound has been reduced to a mere meter in height.

Located in southwestern Ohio, the Great Serpent Mound is one of the most famous earthworks in North America. At 411m (1,348 feet) long, it is the largest serpent effigy in the world. In form, the Great Serpent Mound was perhaps inspired by the constellation recognized by Europeans as Draco, and its coils align with the rising of the stars of Draco just as the setting of the sun on the summer solstice aligns with the egg the serpent is swallowing. To its builders, the Serpent Mound likely represented the Horned Serpent, a ubiquitious figure in the mythos of the Eastern Woodlands. The Horned Serpents are chaotic beings from the Below World and guardians of powerful medicine that provide foresight and success in hunting.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE] The Great Serpent Mound is thought to have been built around AD 1070 by the people of the Fort Ancient Tradition, the ancestors of the Shawnee among others. More recently it has been argued that the Fort Ancient people restored the Serpent Mound at this time, and that it had originally been built a thousand years earlier by the Adena, whose conical burial mounds stand on a nearby hillside.

Standing 30 meters tall and having a volume of 720,000 cubic meters, Monks Mound at Cahokia dwarfs all other earthen pyramids built in the Eastern Woodlands, with a footprint equivalent to that of the Great Pyramid of Giza. Around AD 1050, Cahokia transformed itself from a large, but not particularly unique, village into the largest city the Eastern Woodlands had seen. Looming over the Grand Plaza, Monks Mound was a potent symbol of Cahokia’s might and ability to galvanize its populace. Standing at the crossroads of the continent’s great rivers, Cahokia drew in trade routes from far and wide. Like other Mississippian chiefdoms, it likely demanded tribute from lesser polities such as Kincaid along the Ohio River. Monks Mound got its name from a group of Jesuit monks who lived in the region during the colonial era, and today Cahokia is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Newark Earthworks in Newark, Ohio, consists of two sections of preserved earthworks: the Great Circle Earthworks and the Octagon Earthworks / Observatory Circle, built by the Scioto Hopewell around AD 250. Together the Octagon Earthworks and Observatory Circle form an enormous lunar observatory, aligned with the 18.6 year cycle of lunar standstills. The Great Circle likely hosted elaborate ceremonies that drew in participants from throughout the vast Hopewell Interaction Sphere, a ceremonial and trading network that extended over the whole of eastern North America. Originally, this complex contained the largest earthen enclosures in the world, extending over 3,000 acres. Today, the preserved site covers only 206 acres, and is operated as a state park by the Ohio Historical Society. It has been designated a National Historic Landmark. In 2006, Newark Earthworks was also designated as the "official prehistoric monument of the State of Ohio."
